item.title: Nested tmux over SSH: why Ctrl-k worked through a relay but not directly
item.author: william
item.description:
Ctrl-k reached my remote tmux when I logged in through a relay, but the same key went to local tmux when I connected directly. The loopback login, nb, and nbx all reached the intended SSH server. The problem was how my local helper decided where to send the key.

The fix was to treat known forwarded endpoints differently from a relay. For ports 62222 and 62223, I already knew the destination used Ctrl-k, so I could skip detection. For a relay, I still needed to detect when the second SSH connection started and ended. This follows up on my two-hop tmux setup.

item.title: Nested tmux over SSH: dynamically route Ctrl-k across two hops
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-11-21: I tested real keystrokes through the two-hop login, including the return to the relay shell. Direct logins through my forwarded ports exposed a separate problem: the TCP source port changes in transit, so the observer cannot match the login terminal. See the forwarded-port fix for nb and nbx for the updated helper and test results.

Update 2026-11-15: there were two corrections. Always forwarding for a relay hostname broke local Ctrl-k when no second hop was active. Watching only remote tmux panes then missed my actual ssh → zsh → nb → ta zsh path: the first hop was a plain shell, not a tmux client. The observer now correlates the interactive SSH connection with its remote login terminal and inspects that terminal’s foreground job. Both downloads below are required; reconnect the first SSH login after updating the observer. Hostnames are anonymized.

My local tmux and the tmux behind a second SSH hop both use Ctrl-k. The first remote uses Ctrl-j. I wanted the prefixes to coexist without an extra escape sequence before every command.

The intended mapping is: Ctrl-k stays local until the first remote’s login terminal, or its active tmux pane, runs another SSH connection. Then Ctrl-b controls local tmux and Ctrl-k goes downstream. If a first-remote tmux is attached, Ctrl-j still controls it. Leaving the second connection returns Ctrl-k to local tmux. The live check verified detection of my nested SSH; it was not a complete keyboard test of every transition.

item.title: Lining up the Claude Code status line with my powerlevel10k prompt: padding -2 and a 5-second refresh
item.author: william
item.description:
I keep Claude Code in a tmux pane above a zsh pane, so its status line sits just above my zsh prompt, and the two almost matched. Both used the same powerlevel10k colours and separators, but Claude’s line started 2 columns further in and stopped wherever its text ran out. The zsh line ran the full width of the terminal, so the pair looked misaligned.

The fix was a dotted gap computed from $COLUMNS and "padding": -2, a value the docs don’t mention. Now both prompts start at column 0 and close on the same column, 134 of 135.

item.title: Fixing duplicated tmux status bars and missing icons in Termius on iPhone
item.author: william
item.description:
My tmux status bar looked fine on Linux, but connecting to the same session from Termius on my iPhone left repeated copies of the bar at the bottom of the screen. Moving it to the top was a useful workaround. I wanted to keep it at the bottom and keep the desktop’s colors and useful widgets.

The fix was a compact renderer for clients below 100 columns, followed by a targeted replacement for an icon the phone could not render. This extends my one-job status renderer: the phone still uses one status job, and a desktop attached to the same session keeps its full layout. The app is Termius, although I initially called it Terminus.

item.title: tmux lag, round 2: every status-bar fork froze the server for 30 ms
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-09: I extended this renderer for a 71-column iPhone client: compact text stopped duplicated bottom status rows while keeping the desktop colors and widgets. See the Termius on iPhone follow-up.

Two days after the last fix, my tmux was laggy again, and the server was back at about a quarter of a CPU core. The culprit was the same as last time: the status bar’s #() jobs. This time, though, the number of jobs wasn’t the problem. Each one had become slow, because every job is a fork of the whole tmux server and my server had grown to 1.5 GB.

This post covers how I measured it, where the 1.5 GB came from (mostly the scrollback of three panes), and the fixes. One of them corrects a claim in my previous post.

item.title: Why my tmux was laggy: the status bar was forking a 1.2 GB server 24 times a second
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-02: two days later the lag was back. Each fork of the server had become slow (~30 ms), and one claim below was wrong: passing #{E:#{@quote_cond}} into the job does not work, because tmux does not apply strftime inside a #() command. See round 2.

My tmux had started to feel sluggish. Nothing was broken, it just felt heavy. It turned out the tmux server was using about a third of a CPU core all the time, and nearly all of that went on the status bar. Part of the cost came from the clock workaround in my previous post.

This post covers how I tracked it down, including two wrong guesses, and the fix, which brought the server from ~35% CPU to ~4% without restarting it.

item.title: Linux 时区、系统时间与 tmux 状态栏时间不一致的排查
item.author: william
item.description:
我把 Linux 的时区设成 Asia/Tokyo，又手动设置了系统时间，但 tmux 右侧状态栏仍慢一个小时。例如，系统显示 14:37 JST，tmux 却显示 13:37 CST。问题不在 timedatectl set-time：一个早已启动的 tmux server 仍按旧时区格式化状态栏。

1
2
3
4

sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Tokyo
sudo timedatectl set-ntp false
# aligned to real Asia/Shanghai time
timedatectl set-time "2026-09-26 15:33:00"
